624.title: Hanuman's counsel
624.hook: to comfort Sita, the monkey who just crossed an ocean tells her he's the weakest of Sugriva's army
624.carry: none in the army weaker than me
624.howItsDone: The chudamani, Sita's hair jewel, is a familiar element in Ramayana art and storytelling, and Hanuman's words of reassurance to Sita are often recited by devotees as words of comfort in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: her doubt. Even when Hanuman grew like a mountain, Sita said no, for safety, choice and Rama's honor. Your line: a decision, not a doubt.

Hanuman has to leave Sita in the grove. She's chosen to wait for Rama. Goodbyes like this are the hardest part: you're leaving, they're staying, and you want to say something that lasts after you've gone. Before he goes, she gives him tokens to take back, and he gives her something too: his counsel. A few sentences meant to hold her up until help arrives.
screen: `THE HARDEST PART IS THE GOODBYE.` → `TOKENS FOR RAMA.` → `COUNSEL FOR SITA.`

segments.voice: First, Sita's tokens. She tells Hanuman a private memory only Rama would know. One day at Chitrakuta a crow kept attacking her, and Rama, angry, sent a single blade of grass after it, charged with divine power; the crow found no shelter anywhere until it came back and fell at Rama's feet. Tell him that, she says, and he'll know you met me. Then she unties a jewel from her hair, the chudamani, and gives it to him. And she says plainly that she can hold on only for a month. Then Hanuman counsels her. Don't grieve. Rama and Lakshmana will come soon with Sugriva's army; they will burn Lanka and take you home. And because Sita has asked how monkeys could ever cross this ocean, he adds something surprising. There are many in Sugriva's army stronger than me, and none weaker. If I could cross, how much more easily can they? The monkey who leapt a hundred yojanas, fought Simhika and talked his way past Surasa calls himself the least of the army. Is it true? The story has shown his strength; it's hard to believe. But that's not the point. If Hanuman is the strongest, the rescue depends on one monkey. If he's the weakest, help is enormous, and coming. He makes himself small, so her hope can be large: words shaped to what she most fears.
screen: `THE CROW AND THE BLADE OF GRASS.` · `THE JEWEL FROM HER HAIR.` · `DON'T GRIEVE; RAMA WILL COME.` · then, large: `NONE IN THE ARMY IS WEAKER THAN ME.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone who's waiting for something hard, a diagnosis, a verdict, a return, and gently notice what they most fear. Let a few simple, true words of comfort form, shaped not to what you want to say but to that fear, and breathe them in and out slowly until they feel right.
Hanuman's counsel. His words to Sita before leaving: don't grieve, Rama will come, and there are many in the army stronger than me, and none weaker.
Your line: none in the army weaker than me. Tomorrow, Hanuman counsels himself. Day six hundred twenty-four, done.

625.title: Hanuman's counsel
625.hook: the job is done, and Hanuman could fly home, but first he holds a council with the only advisor present: himself
625.howItsDone: Some teachers of the Sundara Kanda cite Hanuman's deliberation before destroying the grove as a model of a capable envoy, and the four means of statecraft he weighs are a standard idea in classical Indian political thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's counsel to Sita. The crow, the hair jewel, and your line, none in the army weaker than me.
screen: `NONE IN THE ARMY WEAKER THAN ME.`

segments.voice: Hanuman has found Sita, delivered the ring, received the jewel. His mission, as Sugriva gave it, is complete. Going home now would be perfectly fair. Or there's the other question: while I'm here, is there something more this needs? He walks a little way from Sita through the grove, and Valmiki, once again, lets us hear him think it through.

His reasoning comes in steps. First: I've found Sita; that was the work I was given. But a little remains. Rama will have to fight Ravana, and it would help him to know the enemy's strength. Second, he runs through the four classic ways of dealing with an opponent in Indian statecraft: conciliation, gifts, division and force. Conciliation does no good with rakshasas. Gifts mean nothing to those already piled with wealth. People proud of their strength can't be split apart. So only one way is left: a show of strength, to test them and to be brought before Ravana himself. Third, a principle. The one fit for a task, he says, is the one who, given a job, gets many things done, without working against the first. That last clause matters. Hanuman has already secured the main thing: he's found Sita and has her jewel. Nothing he does next can undo that. Only now does he allow himself the risk. So he decides to wreck this beautiful grove, Ravana's pleasure garden, to draw the rakshasas out, see how they fight, and get himself taken to Ravana. Look at his path: in the palace, despair; in the tree, careful speech; with Sita, comfort shaped to her fear; and now, with the job done, strategy. He holds a council in his own head, and then he acts.

626.title: the fight
626.hook: a monkey tears up Ravana's favorite garden, leaving one tree standing, and then announces exactly whose servant he is
626.carry: I am the servant of Rama
626.howItsDone: Hanuman's declaration of victory to Rama and of himself as Rama's servant is recited by devotees, and some see in it the heart of Hanuman's devotion, dāsya, the love of a servant.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's counsel with himself. The task was done, so he weighed the four ways, and your line, do more, without spoiling it.

At dawn, the birds of the ashoka grove start up in alarm. Trees crash down. Pools are churned to mud. Pavilions come apart. Ravana's most beautiful garden is being taken apart by something huge. The guards wake, and they notice something odd. In the middle of the wreckage, one tree is left untouched: the one Sita sits beneath.
screen: `DAWN, AND THE GROVE COMES DOWN.` → `ONE TREE LEFT STANDING.`

segments.voice: The rakshasi guards turn to Sita. Who is that? What did he say to you? Sita gives a clever answer. How would I know? Rakshasas are the ones who change shape at will. You'd know better than I would. She protects Hanuman and gives them nothing. The guards run to Ravana. Furious, he sends a great company of servants, armed and fierce, to capture the monkey. Hanuman is waiting for them on the gateway arch. He grows huge, slaps his arms, and roars a declaration, which Valmiki gives in full. Victory to Rama, mighty in strength, and to Lakshmana. Victory to King Sugriva, protected by Rama. And then: dāso 'haṃ kosalendrasya. I am the servant of the lord of Kosala, Rama. I am Hanuman, son of the wind. Notice what he says first, in the enemy's capital, at the start of a fight. Not his own strength, though he names it. His loyalty. He says whose servant he is before he says who he is. Then the servants rush him. Hanuman snatches up an iron bar from the gateway and drives them back. It's only the first wave; Ravana will send more, each stronger than the last. Hanuman wanted to see Lanka's strength. Lanka is about to show him.
screen: `ONE TREE, AND SITA, SPARED.` · `HOW WOULD I KNOW?` · `I AM THE SERVANT OF RAMA.` · then, large: `THE FIRST WAVE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, simply and without heaviness: whose am I, what do I serve, love or belong to, a family, a cause, a faith, a craft, a friend? Let one answer come and breathe with it, noticing how it feels to name that before you name anything about yourself.
The fight. Hanuman wrecks Ravana's grove but spares Sita's tree, declares himself Rama's servant from the gateway, and drives back the first wave of guards.
Your line: I am the servant of Rama. Tomorrow, Lanka sends its best. See you then.

627.title: the fight
627.hook: Hanuman beats every champion Lanka sends, until one weapon he could escape, and chooses not to
627.howItsDone: Hanuman bound by Indrajit's Brahmastra, and choosing to submit so as to meet Ravana, appears in recitations and dance-dramas, and some tell it as an example of strength that knows when to yield.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fight began. One tree spared, and from the gateway, your line: I am the servant of Rama.

Ravana keeps raising the stakes. After the first wave falls, he sends Jambumali, a fierce warrior. Then seven sons of his ministers, in shining chariots. Then five of his generals. Each time the same news comes back to the palace: the monkey is still on the gate. Then Ravana sends his own young son, Aksha, and Valmiki pauses the fighting to let Hanuman look at the boy.
screen: `JAMBUMALI, THE SEVEN, THE FIVE.` → `THEN RAVANA'S YOUNG SON.`

segments.voice: Hanuman admires Aksha; Valmiki tells us so. The boy is brave and skilled, radiant like the young sun, and Hanuman is reluctant to kill one so young. But Aksha's arrows keep coming, and Hanuman decides an enemy this strong can't be ignored. He kills him. The epic doesn't hide the cost, or Hanuman's hesitation. Now Ravana sends his son Indrajit, whose name means conqueror of Indra. Their duel is long, and neither can wound the other. So Indrajit reaches for the weapon of Brahma, the Brahmastra, and binds Hanuman with it. Hanuman falls, unable to move. Here's the remarkable part. Hanuman knows this weapon. By Brahma's own blessing, it can hold him only a short while. He could wait it out and break free. He chooses to stay down, out of respect for Brahma, and because it serves his purpose: to be brought before Ravana. Then the rakshasas, not trusting the divine weapon, tie him with ropes and bark, and Valmiki says the Brahmastra releases its hold the moment other bonds are added. Indrajit despairs; his own soldiers have undone his weapon. Hanuman keeps playing captive. He lets them drag him through the streets, hitting and jeering, into the hall where Ravana sits on his throne. He fought his way here. Now he's going to talk.
screen: `HANUMAN HESITATES OVER AKSHA.` · `INDRAJIT AND THE BRAHMASTRA.` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY BOUND.` · then, large: `DRAGGED BEFORE RAVANA'S THRONE.`

628.title: the burning
628.hook: a messenger gives the most powerful king in the world good advice, and the king answers by setting the messenger's tail on fire
628.carry: the fire does not burn him
628.howItsDone: The burning of Hanuman's tail and Sita's prayer to Agni are familiar scenes in Ramayana retellings, and Vibhishana's rule that an envoy must not be killed is cited by some teachers as an example of dharma in war.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fight. Aksha, the Brahmastra, and your line, he chooses to stay bound, to reach Ravana.

Hanuman stands tied up before Ravana's throne, and the first thing Valmiki tells us is that Hanuman is impressed. Ravana is magnificent: radiant, crowned, mighty, surrounded by ministers. Hanuman thinks that if this king weren't so unrighteous, he could be the guardian of heaven itself. A minister asks who sent him, and Hanuman answers. Not with threats. With counsel.
screen: `HANUMAN IS IMPRESSED.` → `IF ONLY HE WERE RIGHTEOUS.` → `NOT THREATS, COUNSEL.`

segments.voice: I am Sugriva's envoy, he says, and Rama's messenger. Then he speaks to Ravana as to a king who could still choose well. You know dharma. You've gained great power through austerities. Don't throw it away for another man's wife. Give Sita back to Rama, and you can still live. Ravana's answer is rage: kill him. Then his younger brother Vibhishana speaks up. It is against dharma to kill a messenger. Punish him some other way, but you may not take his life. Ravana gives in, grudgingly. A monkey's tail is precious to him, he says. Set it on fire. So they wrap Hanuman's tail in old cloth, soak it in oil, light it, and parade him through the streets with drums, announcing his crime. The rakshasi guards run to tell Sita. And Sita, in the grove, turns to the fire god, Agni. If I have served my husband faithfully, she prays, if I have any merit at all, be cool to Hanuman. The fire, burning brightly on his tail, does not burn him. Hanuman is astonished: flame, and no pain. He guesses it's Sita's doing, or Rama's power, or his father the wind's friendship with fire. Then he makes himself small, slips the ropes, grows huge again, and climbs to the rooftops, his tail still blazing.
screen: `RETURN SITA AND BE SAVED.` · `AN ENVOY MAY NOT BE KILLED.` · `SITA ASKS AGNI TO BE COOL.` · then, large: `THE FIRE DOES NOT BURN HIM.`

629.title: the burning
629.hook: Lanka goes up in flames, and the monkey who lit it stands on the shore suddenly sick with one question: what if Sita burned too?
629.carry: like a snake shedding its skin
629.howItsDone: Lanka-dahana, the burning of Lanka, is a beloved scene in Ramlila performances and temple art, and Hanuman's self-reproach over anger afterward is often quoted by teachers as a lesson in self-control.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the burning. Counsel refused, an envoy spared, and your line, the fire does not burn him, after Sita asked it to be cool.

Hanuman leaps from rooftop to rooftop with his blazing tail, and the wind, his father, fans every flame. Mansions, towers and gateways catch fire. Valmiki describes Lanka burning like the end of an age. Then Hanuman dips his tail in the sea, stops, and looks back. It's the moment after anger, when the heat drains away and a cold thought arrives: what did I just break?
screen: `LANKA BURNS.` → `HE LOOKS BACK.` → `THE MOMENT AFTER ANGER.`

segments.voice: Valmiki notes one careful detail. Hanuman spares one house in all of Lanka: Vibhishana's, the brother who spoke up for him. Then the cold thought. Sita. Did the fire reach the grove? Did I burn the very person I came to save? Hanuman is horrified, and he turns on his own anger with words worth keeping. Blessed is the one who can throw off anger the moment it rises, the way a snake sheds its old skin. An angry person can do anything: harm a teacher, say what should never be said. He calls himself a fool who has ruined Rama's whole mission in a moment of fury. The hero of the Sundara Kanda, at the height of his triumph, condemns his own temper. Then he notices good omens around him, and hears voices in the sky, the celestial beings called charanas, marveling: Lanka is burned, and yet Janaki, Sita, is unharmed. Relief floods him. And in Valmiki, Hanuman himself sees why: Sita is guarded by her own power, the same Sita who asked the fire to be cool to him. Fire, he reasons, does not burn fire. He goes back one last time to the ashoka grove, sees her alive with his own eyes, bows, and takes his leave. He'd reached the edge of what anger can do, and it frightened him. The fire was a victory. The fear afterward was the wisdom.
screen: `VIBHISHANA'S HOUSE IS SPARED.` · `WHAT IF SITA BURNED?` · `LIKE A SNAKE SHEDDING ITS SKIN.` · then, large: `SITA IS UNHARMED.`

630.title: the return
630.hook: on the far shore, a hungry, anxious army hears a roar coming over the sea, and knows from the sound alone how it went
630.howItsDone: In Sundara Kanda recitations, the return of Hanuman and the monkeys' joy on Mount Mahendra is read with delight, and some families mark the completion of a recitation with celebration and sweets.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the burning. Lanka in flames, Hanuman's horror at his own anger, and your line, like a snake shedding its skin.

On the northern shore, Angada, Jambavan and the whole search party have been waiting, watching the sea the way people watch the doors at an arrivals gate, trying to read a face before it reaches them. Then they hear it. A roar, far off over the water, getting louder. Jambavan listens and says: that's the roar of someone who has succeeded.
screen: `WATCHING THE SEA.` → `A ROAR OVER THE WATER.` → `THE SOUND OF SUCCESS.`

segments.voice: The flight back begins like the first one. Hanuman climbs a mountain on Lanka's shore, Arishta, and presses down to spring; Valmiki says the mountain sinks into the earth. Then he's in the air, crossing the sky like a great cloud, and Valmiki makes the sky an ocean: the moon a water lily, the sun a waterbird, the clouds its water weed. Nearing Mahendra, he roars, so the others will know before he lands. They hear, and they know. The monkeys leap from tree to tree, waving branches, delirious. Hanuman lands among them, and they crowd around him with fruit and roots, touching him, cheering. He bows to Jambavan and Angada and tells them in a few words: I've seen her. She's alive. Then, at Jambavan's urging, he sits down and tells them everything, from the beginning. That closes the week, and nearly the whole adventure. Tokens in the grove: the crow story, the hair jewel, Hanuman calling himself the least of the army. His council with himself, and the grove torn up. I am the servant of Rama. Aksha, Indrajit, and the bonds he chose. Counsel refused, and a tail on fire that didn't burn. Lanka burning, and a hero sick with fear at his own anger. And now the shore, where a roar arrives before the news.
screen: `ARISHTA SINKS AS HE LEAPS.` · `THE SKY LIKE AN OCEAN.` · `THE ROAR, AND THE KNOWING.` · then, large: `I'VE SEEN HER. SHE'S ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone came home with good news, or you did, and the moment just before the words, when the face or the voice already told you. Breathe in that relief that arrives before the details, let it fill the chest, then let the breath go out slowly, as if you were landing.
The return. Hanuman's leap back from Mount Arishta, his roar over the sea, and the search party who know, from the sound alone, that he has found Sita.
Your line: the roar, and the knowing. Tomorrow, a honey forest in trouble. A full week, done.
